headline: Elon Musk Gave $158M to the GOP Group Helping Ken Paxton. Polls Still Call It a Coin Flip.
dek: Texans are already voting, and a 2,000-voter poll has Talarico up 48-46, inside the margin of error. Here's where Musk's money went and what's false.
bottomLine: FEC filings confirm that Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September, and that money went to a new group running ads for Ken Paxton. Polls show James Talarico narrowly ahead, but the leads are inside the margin of error, and Texas polls have underestimated Republicans before. Nobody knows the outcome. The money, the polling and the false rumors spread about the race are all documented.

body: Texans started voting Monday, and the most expensive question in American politics now has a name attached: Elon Musk. FEC filings show Musk wrote two checks to the Senate Leadership Fund in September, $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. Each time, the Senate GOP's flagship super PAC moved the same amount the next day into Texas PAC, a new affiliate buying ads for Ken Paxton and against James Talarico.

All that money is chasing a race that, by most measures, is a coin flip. A University of Houston Hobby School poll of 2,000 likely voters, taken Oct. 10-14, has Talarico at 48% and Paxton at 46%, inside the ±2.19-point margin of error. Fox News' late-September poll showed a similar 51-49 split. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994.

Talarico isn't short of money either. His campaign committee reported $60.2 million in third-quarter receipts to the FEC, and the campaign says the total is $64 million counting its joint fundraising arm. He had $14.6 million on hand on Sept. 30, against $4.9 million for Paxton's committee. But outside spending dwarfs both campaigns: AdImpact data cited by the Texas Tribune shows outside groups had spent more than $217 million on ads by the end of September.

Paxton himself sounds uneasy about the help. In audio from a Sept. 24 lobbyist-hosted lunch in Washington, first published by Politico, the attorney general said, "I've never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign." His campaign says he meant the legal wall between campaigns and super PACs.

The race has also been a test of how fast falsehoods spread. While Talarico was off the trail with the flu, conservative influencers on X spread a claim that he'd been treated at an Ohio mental health facility. The facility denied it, and the AP, Snopes and FactCheck.org all rated it false. Earlier, Paxton's campaign ran an AI-generated ad depicting Talarico reading from a fictional Bible, which FactCheck.org said stripped his real remarks of context and added words he never said.

Then there's the debate that isn't happening. Talarico has accepted several network invitations. As of mid-October, Paxton had accepted none, even after President Trump publicly called for a debate. That puts Texas on track for its first Senate race without a debate in about a quarter century.

Prediction markets lean Talarico. Kalshi traders put his odds at about 62% as of Oct. 20. But Tangle notes that polls underestimated Republicans in Texas in 2024 and 2022, and early voting runs only through Oct. 30. The $158 million question will be answered on Nov. 3.

headline: The Senate Voted 86-11 to Squeeze Putin. Trump Signed It, Then Waived Most of It.
dek: Two days before new Russia sanctions were set to bite, Trump set most aside with no end date. Older sanctions remain. Top Republicans are objecting.
bottomLine: On Oct. 16, Trump signed an order waiving most of the new tariffs and sanctions in the Graham Act, using a national-interest waiver the law itself provides. The waiver has no end date. Older U.S. sanctions on Russia stay in place. The move came a week after a deal to buy Russian diesel, and Republicans and Democrats alike have condemned it. Whether it helps peace talks or lowers fuel prices is unproven.

body: The Senate voted 86-11 to hit Vladimir Putin's economy with sweeping new tariffs and sanctions. On Sept. 18, President Trump signed it. On Friday, Oct. 16, two days before most of its provisions were set to take effect, he signed an executive order setting them aside.

The order invokes the law's own escape hatch, a Section 115 waiver allowed when the president certifies it is "in the national interests of the United States." It waives tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods, up to 100% secondary tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, and a long list of new sanctions. It sets no end date: the waivers last until the president or secretary of state decides otherwise. Sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain.

The timing points to diesel. On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Putin to move Russian diesel onto world markets, and Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, authorizing Russian diesel transactions through April 2027. NBC reports diesel prices have climbed almost 70% since the Iran war began in February. CBS calculates the U.S. purchase at about 2.2 million barrels, just over half of a single day's U.S. diesel use.

Republicans didn't stay quiet. Sen. Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible." Sen. Ted Cruz said, "I think it was a mistake." Sen. John Cornyn said Graham "would be appalled." Even Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to her late brother's seat and is now on the ballot, said she "would choose to keep the pressure on Russia." Democrats including Chuck Schumer and Richard Blumenthal went further, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the decision wrong.

The White House says enforcing the sanctions now would "impede ongoing U.S. efforts" to negotiate peace. Trump called it "a very good decision." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president wants 60 days to analyze the impact, although the order itself contains no such clock.

Can Congress stop it? Not before the election. Both chambers are in recess until after Nov. 3, and the waiver section requires only a certification and a report, not a vote. Rep. Gregory Meeks has introduced a bill to block the diesel deal, but it can't move until lawmakers return.

Traders aren't betting on a quick payoff for the peace argument. Polymarket puts a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire agreement by Dec. 31 at about 16.5%, and gives roughly 30% odds that Russian diesel actually lands in the U.S. by the end of November.

stat.label: Senate vote for the Russia sanctions law Trump signed, then mostly waived on Oct. 16

tldr.what: Trump signed a tough Russia sanctions law Sept. 18. On Oct. 16, before most of it kicked in, he used its built-in waiver to set those parts aside.
tldr.why: The White House says enforcing it would hurt Ukraine peace talks, and it followed a Russian diesel deal the administration says will lower fuel prices. Neither benefit is proven yet.
tldr.truth: Verified: it's legal under the law's own waiver, has no end date, and older sanctions stay. Misleading: 'Trump lifted the sanctions.' Unproven: it helps peace talks.

newAngle: Rubio says the president wants 60 days to study the impact, but the order itself sets no clock, and Treasury's diesel license (General License 135) runs all the way to April 7, 2027. body: Twenty-two days before the midterms, federal agents showed up at a sitting congresswoman's home. On Oct. 12, Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home under a warrant the Justice Department says was judicially authorized, as part of "an ongoing federal criminal investigation." Eight days later, there are no charges, and DOJ hasn't publicly said what it suspects.

Reporting from several outlets, citing people familiar with the probe, points to immigration paperwork. Investigators are reportedly looking at whether Omar's late father lied or left information off his forms, and whether Omar was 17 or 18 when he became a citizen in 2000. Omar says she became a citizen before she turned 18. Grand jury subpoenas went to relatives, including, per The New York Times, her sister Sahra Noor. Agents took Omar's cellphone, and The Washington Post reported they took her passport too.

The search itself is now in dispute. In an Oct. 16 letter, Omar's lawyers say agents ignored a magistrate judge's instructions meant to protect her rights as a member of Congress: notify the House General Counsel and hand her the warrant at the start. DOJ says the letter is "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and that it followed every court order.

Administration officials haven't been shy. Border czar Tom Homan told Fox News on Oct. 18 that denaturalization "could happen" "if the evidence points that way," and that he'd been told investigators have "a strong case," while saying he didn't know the specifics. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has repeated the claim that Omar married her brother, which Snopes rates unfounded and for which no public evidence exists.

Trump said the search had nothing to do with him and deferred to DOJ, but days earlier he told a Tennessee rally that "JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly." House Democratic leaders called the search "corrupt weaponization." NBC notes DOJ has no blanket 60-day pre-election blackout, but its policy says investigative steps shouldn't be timed to affect an election.

Some of this has come up before. A 2019 inquiry into Omar's immigration history found insufficient evidence for a full investigation, The Washington Post reported. A 2019 request by her staff to change her listed birth year with the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library is documented, but even Fox News notes it "does not establish that Omar falsified immigration records."
Traders are skeptical of a fast case. Polymarket puts federal charges by Oct. 31 at about 6.5% and by Dec. 31 at about 22.5%. Omar's Minneapolis seat isn't considered at risk on Nov. 3.

tldr.what: On Oct. 12, federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home with a judge-approved warrant. They took her phone, reports say. No charges have been filed.
tldr.why: It happened three weeks before the midterms, and border czar Tom Homan says stripping her citizenship "could happen" if evidence supports it. None has been released.
tldr.truth: Verified: a judge-approved search, grand jury subpoenas to relatives, and zero charges. Widely reported: the probe concerns family immigration paperwork. No public evidence proves wrongdoing.

newAngle: The 'strong case' line behind many headlines is secondhand: Homan said he'd been told that, and that he didn't have the evidence specifics himself. Even Fox News, which has led on the birth-year question, notes that the 2019 birth-year record change "does not establish that Omar falsified immigration records."
